kurz: How share-based compensation, capital increases and convertible bonds increase the number of shares, how the dilution of earnings per share can be calculated and what adjusted figures leave out.

bloecke.md:
A shareholder's stake in a company can shrink in two ways without the shareholder selling any shares. The first is a capital increase, which is reported publicly. The second is the issue of shares as part of pay. This happens quarter after quarter in small amounts and therefore attracts little attention.

For earnings per share, both have the same effect, because in both cases the number of shares, that is the denominator, rises. A company can increase its profit by 85% over eight years and still report only 46% more profit per share. The part of the profit attributable to the additional shares goes to new shareholders, mostly the company's own employees and the management board.

## Expense without a cash outflow

Share-based compensation includes options and above all restricted stock units (RSUs), that is, promises to receive shares after a waiting period. Under IFRS 2, this compensation must be recognised as an expense. It is measured at fair value on the grant date and spread over the vesting period. The offsetting entry is made directly in equity; no cash leaves the company. In separate financial statements under the HGB (Commercial Code), the treatment is disputed. Capital-market-oriented parent companies, however, prepare their consolidated financial statements under IFRS (Section 315e HGB), so IFRS 2 is what matters for investors.

Because no money flows, the expense is added back to profit in the cash flow statement under the indirect method, just like depreciation. Operating cash flow, and with it [[Free cash flow|free cash flow]], therefore comes out higher than profit. This is arithmetically correct but economically misleading, because the work was still paid for, with the existing shareholders' stakes instead of with money.

Share-based compensation is paid with shares instead of money. If it is stripped out of earnings without also looking at the growing share count, these costs no longer appear anywhere. They can only be measured reliably by the diluted share count over five to ten years.

bloecke.unter: The same amount appears as an expense in the income statement, is added back in the cash flow and is stripped out a second time in adjusted earnings, while the share count rises at the same time.

bloecke.md:
## Calculating dilution

IAS 33 requires listed companies to disclose basic and diluted earnings per share. The diluted figure assumes that all outstanding rights to new shares had already been exercised.

For options, the treasury stock method applies. Exercise is assumed, the cash inflow from the exercise prices is calculated, and this cash is used to buy back own shares notionally at the average stock market price for the year. Only the excess of new shares has a dilutive effect. For convertible bonds, the if-converted method applies. Here the new shares go into the denominator and the interest saved, after tax, goes into the numerator. Instruments that would increase earnings per share as a result are disregarded, because the calculation is meant to show dilution and not to improve earnings.

bloecke.titel: Diluted share count of a model company (calculation under IAS 33)
zeilen: + RSUs granted but not yet issued

bloecke.md: On exercise, the options bring in 6.0 × 20 = €120 million. At €50, this amount notionally buys back 2.4 million shares, so that a net 3.6 million shares are dilutive. The convertible bond saves €4.5 million of interest, €3.15 million after 30% tax, and creates 5.0 million new shares. That is €0.63 per new share. This figure is below the diluted earnings per share obtained without the bond. The bond is therefore dilutive and is included. The denominator rises by 12.6%, and earnings per share fall by 9.8%.

bloecke.formel: Dilution rate = (diluted share count − basic share count) / basic share count
bloecke.erklaerung: In the example, this gives 12.6 / 100 = 12.6%. More informative than this figure at a single reporting date is the annual net change in the diluted share count, because it combines grants, exercises and buybacks in one number. Dilution of 3% a year looks small, but over ten years it reduces a shareholder's stake by around a quarter.
variablen: weighted average of the shares actually outstanding

bloecke.titel: Limits of the diluted share count
bloecke.md:
- It only covers rights that have already been granted. The grants of the coming years appear in no balance sheet, even though they occur as regularly as the other salary payments.
- Out-of-the-money options, whose exercise price is above the share price, are disregarded. As soon as the share price rises, they are counted again. Reported dilution is therefore lowest in years with a weak share price.
- Authorised and conditional capital (Sections 202 and 192 AktG, Stock Corporation Act) set the framework for future shares. They are stated in the notes and in the articles of association and are not included in the denominator.

bloecke.titel: Profit, earnings per share and share count (illustrative calculation, index 100)
bloecke.unter: With profit growth of 8% and net dilution of 3% a year, profit is 85% higher after eight years, but earnings per share only 46% higher.

bloecke.md:
## Share buybacks as an offset

Many companies buy back roughly as many of their own shares each year as they issue to employees. The share count then stays constant and no longer shows any dilution. The costs, however, remain. A buyback that merely offsets grants is, in economic terms, cash compensation paid after the fact. It is booked, however, in financing cash flow and not in operating cash flow. The authorisation for buybacks is granted by the general meeting for at most five years and at most 10% of the share capital (Section 71(1) no. 8 AktG). Whether buybacks create value beyond that is a separate question. The only point here is that they pay the costs of share-based compensation and do not eliminate them.

The model company from the table has a share price of €54, 112.6 million diluted shares, a market capitalisation of around €6.08 billion, revenue of €1,500 million and share-based compensation of €84 million.

- Operating cash flow of €420 million minus capital expenditure of €90 million gives €330 million of free cash flow, or 5.4% of market capitalisation.
- This cash flow includes the €84 million as an add-back. Deducting it again leaves €246 million, which is 4.0%.
- To offset the dilution, the company would have to buy back around 1.56 million shares at €54 for €84 million. That is 1.4% of the share count per year.

Both approaches lead to the same result. Either way, the compensation costs the shareholders €84 million.

## Capital increase and subscription right

An ordinary capital increase is resolved by the general meeting with at least three quarters of the share capital represented (Section 182 AktG). Every shareholder has a statutory subscription right (Section 186(1) AktG). The shareholder may subscribe for as many new shares as are needed to keep their percentage holding unchanged. Shareholders who subscribe or sell their subscription rights are not economically diluted. A shareholder who lets the deadline pass without acting loses both percentage holding and money.

In practice, there are three ways of shortening the procedure. The simplified exclusion of subscription rights allows a cash capital increase without subscription rights if the issue price is close to the stock market price (Section 186(3) sentence 4 AktG). The Future Financing Act (Zukunftsfinanzierungsgesetz) raised the limit for this from 10% to 20% of the share capital. Authorised capital empowers the management board in advance for at most five years and at most half of the share capital (Section 202 AktG). Conditional capital serves conversion rights, the preparation of business combinations and employee plans (Section 192 AktG). How many shares a company may issue without a further resolution of the general meeting is therefore stated in the notes and the articles of association. It cannot be read from the share price chart.

Share price before the issue €54.00, subscription ratio 4:1, subscription price €39.00.

- The theoretical price afterwards is (4 × 54 + 39) / 5 = €51.00.
- The value of one subscription right is (54 − 39) / 5 = €3.00. This corresponds to the price markdown.
- A shareholder with four old shares who subscribes for one new share then owns 5 of 125 million shares instead of 4 of 100 million. Their percentage holding stays the same.
- A shareholder who does nothing holds four shares at €51 instead of €54, that is €12 less. In addition, their percentage holding falls by a fifth.

Selling the subscription rights triggers tax. Under the flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer), subscription rights are treated as having acquisition costs of zero (Section 20(4a) EStG, Income Tax Act). Once the [[Saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag)|saver's allowance (Sparerpauschbetrag)]] has been used up, €2.21 of the €3.00 remains after 26.375% flat-rate withholding tax including solidarity surcharge. The tax amount is not lost for good, however. The acquisition costs of the old shares remain unchanged, so the later capital gain is correspondingly lower. The tax is therefore brought forward, and no additional loss arises.

In a capital increase from company funds (Kapitalerhöhung aus Gesellschaftsmitteln, Section 207 AktG), reserves are converted into share capital. Existing shareholders receive bonus shares in proportion to their holding. Substance and percentage holding stay the same; the market value is merely spread over more shares. Economically this corresponds to a share split, and under the Capital Increase Tax Act (Kapitalerhöhungsteuergesetz) it is not capital income. A capital increase against contributions in kind, used to pay for a takeover in shares, by contrast dilutes immediately and in full. Whether it pays off depends solely on what value the company receives in return for the new shares.

## Convertible bonds

A convertible bond is a bond with the right to exchange it for shares of the issuer. Its issue and the existing shareholders' subscription right are governed by Section 221 AktG, and it is serviced from conditional capital. For the company, the advantage lies in the low coupon. A company that offers conversion at a price 30% or 40% above the current share price (conversion premium) pays noticeably less interest in return. It pays for the interest saving by selling a call option on its own shares. If the share price rises, the bondholders convert, and the existing shareholders bear the dilution. This happens precisely when issuing new shares at the fixed conversion price costs the existing shareholders the most.

For private investors on the buying side, the tax position is as follows. Interest is capital income (Section 20(1) no. 7 EStG). The conversion itself does not trigger taxation, and the acquisition costs of the bond carry over to the shares (Section 20(4a) EStG).

## Adjusted figures

Almost every larger group reports its own figures alongside the IFRS numbers, for example adjusted [[EBITDA]], adjusted EPS or non-GAAP operating income. Such figures are neither prohibited nor inherently dishonest. They are classed as alternative performance measures and are subject to the ESMA guidelines, which have applied since 3 July 2016. These require a clear definition, a reconciliation to the closest IFRS figure, a comparison with the previous year and a consistent method of calculation. In addition, the figures must not be presented more prominently than the audited figures. For financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2027, IFRS 18 additionally requires formal disclosure of management-defined performance measures.

In the adjusted accounts of American technology companies, share-based compensation is the most common single item. The justification given is that it is non-cash and therefore not operational. Since the 1990s, Buffett has countered that options are a form of compensation and that compensation is an expense that belongs in the calculation of earnings.

bloecke.md: The figures in the adjusted presentation break no rule, but they are not audited either. A P/E of 17.9 cannot be compared with that of an industrial company without significant share-based compensation, because the two measure different things. Across the market as a whole, too, ratios such as the P/E regularly come out considerably lower when based on estimated earnings than when based on reported earnings.

bloecke.titel: P/E on reported and on expected earnings (US, January 2026)
bloecke.unter: Damodaran aggregates all companies listed in the US, including those making losses, which pushes the trailing figures up sharply; the S&P 500 itself stood at a trailing P/E of 26.64 on 13 October 2026. The gap between the two series is therefore only partly due to adjustments; it results from growth expectations, aggregation and the fact that estimates are almost always based on adjusted earnings.

schritte.titel: Record the share count over ten years
schritte.text: Enter the diluted share count from ten annual reports in one column and the annual change next to it. A net increase of more than 2% should be explainable by the business model.
Divide share-based compensation by revenue and by operating cash flow. If the second figure is persistently above 15%, reported free cash flow is not suitable as a basis for valuation.

schritte.titel: Set buybacks against the share count
schritte.text: Compare the year's buyback volume with the change in the share count. If the share count barely falls despite large buybacks, the buyback is financing the compensation.
Check which items are adjusted, in how many of the last five years the same items appeared and whether income is adjusted as well as expenses.

schritte.titel: Check the notes for future shares
schritte.text: Look up authorised and conditional capital, outstanding options with their exercise prices and RSUs, and the conversion prices and maturities of outstanding convertible bonds.

bloecke.titel: Statements to check against the numbers
bloecke.md:
- If the same items have appeared under *adjusted for special items* for years, they are recurring costs.
- *We are buying back shares* says little as long as it is not stated which part of it merely offsets grants to employees.
- *The capital increase strengthens the balance sheet*, but at the expense of the existing owners. What matters is the issue price and what happens to the money.

mitnehmen: Earnings per share depend on profit and on the share count; decisions about the share count are made frequently, but it receives less attention than profit.
Share-based compensation causes no cash outflow, but it dilutes shareholders' stakes and at the same time makes operating cash flow come out higher.
Dilution can be measured by the development of the diluted share count over several years; the figure for a single financial year is not enough for this.
The subscription right fully offsets a capital increase, but only for shareholders who subscribe or sell the right in time.
Adjusted figures are permitted and regulated, but not audited, so the reconciliation to the IFRS figure deserves more attention than the highlighted figure.

begriffe.text: Earnings per share on the assumption that all outstanding rights to new shares had already been exercised, that is options, employee shares and conversion rights. Under IAS 33 it must be disclosed alongside the basic figure.

Calculation rule for options in diluted earnings per share. The cash inflow from the exercise prices is used to buy back own shares notionally at the average share price for the year. Only the new shares in excess of this increase the share count.
Remuneration in shares or options. Under IFRS 2 it is measured at fair value on the grant date and recognised as an expense over the vesting period, even though no cash flows out.

Right of an existing shareholder, in a capital increase, to subscribe for as many new shares as are needed to keep their percentage holding unchanged (Section 186 AktG). Its theoretical value corresponds to the price markdown of the issue.

Capital increase resolved by the general meeting to service conversion and option rights, to prepare business combinations or for employee plans (Section 192 AktG). The shares only come into existence when the rights are exercised.

Figures defined by the company itself alongside the IFRS financial statements, for example adjusted EPS or adjusted EBITDA. The ESMA guidelines require a definition, a reconciliation to the IFRS figure and consistent use.
